To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the paravermis of the cerebellum is involved in the computation of the velocity vectors required to achieve co‐ordinated arm movements.
the discharge rate of Purkinje cells in the cerebellar paravermal cortex is correlated with the direction and speed of movement, and that these cells fire earlier in the preferred direction.

the discharge of cerebellar neurone activity is more closely related to arm velocity than to position or acceleration and that this activity is modulated prior to movement onset, in some instances by up to 240 ms.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the parietal lobe in the control of reaching and grasping movements.
the role of cerebellar cortex in the control of arm movements.
the function of the cerebellum, which is the part of the brain that controls the movements of the body.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the paravermis is involved in computing the vectors of movement of the whole arm and that the preferred direction of each neurone corresponds to a preferred direction of movement of the arm.

the cerebellum is involved in computing the vector velocity required for achieving properly co‐ordinated movements, but that the cerebellar cortex is also involved in computing other aspects of movement, such as the timing of movement, and the direction of movement.
the paravermis is involved in computing the vector of the arm movement, and that this vector is computed from the vectorial sum of the vectors of each joint movement.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

(i) The cerebellum is involved in the control of movement in the sense that the discharge of movement‐related neurones in the paravermal cortex is related to the velocity of the movement; (ii) this velocity information is used by the cerebellum to generate a movement vector, which is used to guide the movement; and (iii) the movement vector is generated by combining information about the velocity and position of the moving limb
the cerebellum is involved in computing velocity vectors and that these velocity vectors are used to control arm movements.
the cerebellum may play a key role in the computation and storage of movement‐related vectors, which can be retrieved and applied to a wide variety of movements.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cerebellum is not involved in motor learning, but is instead involved in motor execution.
we have shown that the paravermis of the cerebellum is involved in the planning, execution, and control of movements.
the paravermis is involved in the control of the arm as a whole and not just the distal segments.
